questions.prompt: What are the four vertices of the Diamond Model?
questions.explanation: The model asserts these are always connected: an adversary uses a capability over some infrastructure against a victim.

questions.prompt: Which pivot most directly converts one compromised host into an accurate incident scope?
options: Infrastructure to other Victims -- checking which of your other hosts contacted the expanded infrastructure set
questions.explanation: Scoping is a pivoting exercise, and expanding from known infrastructure back across your own estate is what finds the hosts nobody flagged.

questions.prompt: Why is the Adversary vertex often unnecessary in enterprise DFIR?
options: It is always known in advance
You can scope, contain, and remediate completely by pivoting across Capability, Infrastructure, and Victim -- attribution is a threat-intel output, not an IR prerequisite
Attribution is illegal for private organizations
The other three vertices are less reliable
questions.explanation: Treating attribution as a prerequisite delays the work that actually matters, since remediation does not depend on naming the group.

questions.prompt: How does the Diamond Model relate to ATT&CK?
options: They are competing frameworks; you should choose one
They are complementary -- ATT&CK describes techniques by tactic, while Diamond describes entities and the relationships between them
ATT&CK is a subset of the Diamond Model
questions.explanation: A single event can be located in a kill chain phase, mapped to an ATT&CK technique, and expressed as a Diamond event -- each answering a different question.
